list.listitem: Always include evaluation and documentation of distal neurovascular status in the physical examination. C
If x-ray is warranted, obtain three-view foot series and/or dedicated phalanx series to evaluate each component and angulation of potential fracture. C
Always consider Lisfranc fracture dislocation at base of metatarsals or Jones fracture of the fifth metatarsal because they may require surgical intervention. C
Most acute nondisplaced metatarsal fractures may be effectively managed with either a hard shoe or soft elastic dressing and progressive weight bearing. B
Most metatarsal shaft stress fractures do not require immobilization but rather heal well with discontinuation of the offending impact activity for 6 to 8 weeks. C

For acute management, the majority of lesser toe fractures only require treatment with buddy taping and a rigid sole for 4-6 weeks. Great toe fractures are generally treated with a short leg walking boot or cast with toe plate for 2-3 weeks, then transitioned to a rigid-sole shoe for an additional 3-4 weeks. B

background.definition: Acute fracture: fracture resulting from a single traumatic event. Stress fracture: partial or complete bone fracture that results from repeated application of stress lower than the stress required to fracture the bone in a single loading. Lisfranc fracture dislocation: disruption of the osteoligamentous restraints at the tarsal-metatarsal (T-MT) joints; occur most commonly at the base of the first and second metatarsals. Intra-articular fracture: fracture that extends into a joint surface. Avulsion fracture: fragment of bone pulled off by ligament or tendon.

list.listitem: Toe (phalanx) fractures are the most common fracture of the foot, with lesser toe fractures being about twice as common as great toe fractures.
The calcaneus is the most commonly fractured tarsal bone (2% of all fractures); 75% are intra-articular and 25% are extra-articular.
Thirty-five percent of all stress fractures involve the navicular.
Metatarsal fractures make up 35% of all foot fractures and 5% to 6% of fractures encountered in primary care.
Nine percent to 23% of all stress fractures involve the metatarsals.
Acute: direct trauma or twisting force to the bone
Stress: repetitive load
Lateral process of the talus fractures: common in snowboarders
Talar dome fractures may occur with inversion injury
Navicular stress fractures: runners or track athletes
Fifth metatarsal styloid avulsion fracture: occurs frequently with pivot shifting in football or basketball via ankle inversion with plantar flexion of the foot
Lisfranc: downward directed force over a planted, plantar-flexed foot
Following an acute fracture, there is an initial inflammatory response as evidenced by pain, erythema, swelling, and ecchymosis.
This stimulates a reparative process in which osteoblasts lay down new bone matrix with the resultant formation of a fracture callus.
The final process is that of remodeling, whereby excess callus is resorbed by osteoclasts and immature bone is replaced by lamellar bone.

Use Ottawa Foot Rules to determine need for films. A
Stress fractures will often not be evident on plain radiograph until approximately 2 to 8 weeks after onset of symptoms. B
The use of musculoskeletal ultrasonography may be considered to diagnose metatarsal and other fractures of the foot and toes. C

list.listitem: Pain, swelling, and difficulty with ambulation or bearing weight accompany most foot fractures.

Physical examination should include: palpation of metatarsal base, shaft, and head; examination of proximal tarsometatarsal and distal metatarsophalangeal joints; and assessment of neurovascular status and nail bed injury.

A clinical decision rule is useful in determining need for foot films and clinical decision rules are based on the ability to stand on foot at the time of injury and in the emergency department, pain over fifth metatarsal, and pain over navicular bone.

Consider stress fracture in any patient with foot pain who reports a recent increase in intensity or duration of activity. The onset is often insidious and is aggravated by sprinting, jumping, and pushing off.
Palpate the base of the fifth metatarsal in patients with inversion ankle injuries, and if tenderness is present, obtain radiographs to rule out an avulsion fracture.
The mechanism of injury and/or type and level of training for sports/fitness can provide key diagnostic clues as to the etiology of the presenting complaint.
Injury to the Lisfranc joint is likely if the patient has T-MT joint tenderness and inability to stand on the toes.

Plain film radiographs are the initial test of choice for essentially all suspected fractures. For most foot fractures, this includes AP, lateral, and oblique views. Comparison views are helpful in the measurement of normal anatomic angles and ruling out anatomic variants. Tenderness at the base of the fifth metatarsal should warrant ankle radiographs (AP, lateral, and mortise views) if no fracture is seen on standard foot series.

Recent studies have demonstrated that musculoskeletal ultrasonography and traditional radiography have comparable accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity in the diagnosis of foot and ankle fractures. Although operator-dependent, ultrasound is a reasonable tool for evaluation as it is quick, easily accessible, and does not expose the patient to radiation. Ultrasonography may be preferred when patients present within a few hours of injury with associated edema or in the early prediction of impaired fracture healing when radiography is not as sensitive.
MRI may reveal a defined fracture line even in very early stages of a stress fracture. When clinical suspicion remains high in the setting of negative radiography, MRI may be obtained.

Widening of the space between the bases of the first and second metatarsals of more than 2 mm suggests injury to the Lisfranc joint. Weight-bearing plain radiographs or further imaging with MRI or CT is essential if clinical suspicion remains high for Lisfranc injury after negative plain x-rays, because standard foot series is only 50% sensitive for detection of Lisfranc injuries.

If a navicular stress fracture is suspected, obtain conventional radiographs of the weight-bearing foot as the initial study. These may be normal in the acute phase. Additional studies may then be considered, such as CT, MRI, and bone scan. MRI evaluation of navicular stress fractures provides a sensitive method of evaluation with more specificity than bone scan.

Appropriate radiographic views for calcaneus fractures include lateral, axial, and dorsoplantar views. CT has been shown to improve classification of calcaneal fractures and is often needed to exclude articular surface involvement and determine the extent of the fracture.
The well-validated Ottawa Ankle and Foot Rule can help determine whether radiographs are needed in a patient complaining of foot pain.
See algorithms for a suggested approach to the evaluation of patients with suspected metatarsal fracture and suspected proximal fifth metatarsal fracture see and
See and for treatment recommendations regarding metatarsal and tarsal fractures respectively.
Most acute nondisplaced metatarsal fractures may be effectively managed with either a hard shoe or soft elastic dressing and progressive weight bearing. B
Most metatarsal shaft stress fractures do not require immobilization and heal well with discontinuation of the offending impact activity for 6 to 8 weeks. C

For acute Jones fractures in recreationally active patients, early intramedullary screw fixation results in lower failure rates and shorter times to both clinical union and return to sports than nonweight-bearing short-leg casting (NWBSLC), based on multiple RCTs. A
Greater toe fractures may be treated with a short leg walking boot or cast for 2-3 weeks, then a rigid-sole shoe for an additional 3-4 weeks. B
Treatment for the majority of lesser toe fractures only requires buddy taping and a rigid-sole for 4-6 weeks with progressive ambulation as tolerated. B
Any patient with an open fracture, vascular compromise, compartment syndrome, devitalized skin, or acute neurologic deficit should be referred for emergent evaluation. C

Due to the concern that these agents may delay bone healing, NSAIDs are not recommended in the treatment of completed fractures (or) stress fractures at higher risk of nonunion. However, analysis of recent literature suggests that low-dose/short-duration NSAID use does not appear to have irreversible effects on bone healing or affect union rates. Further prospective studies in humans are needed to form a definite consensus regarding the use of NSAIDs.

A Cochrane review identified eight studies with 1106 participants that compared antibiotics with placebo for open fracture of the extremities. They found good evidence that antibiotics reduced the risk of early infection (RR 0.43; 95% CI, 0.29-0.65), corresponding to a 7% absolute risk reduction.

Another Cochrane review found 11 trials with 572 participants comparing different methods of cleaning and dressing percutaneous pin sites. Studies were generally small, heterogeneous regarding interventions and outcomes, and poorly designed. A polyhexamethylene biguanide gauze reduced infections compared to a plain gauze (1% vs 4.5% infection rates; NNT = 30).
Surgery is indicated for select fractures; see and .

A systematic review of six RCTs and four observational studies with 891 patients found that surgical therapy was marginally more effective than non-surgical therapy in terms of return to work following intra-articular calcaneal fractures, but there were more complications with surgery.

An RCT randomized 151 patients with acute, displaced intra-articular calcaneal fracture to operative or non-operative treatment. After 2 years, there was no difference in the Kerr-Atkins score for pain and function, or in any other outcomes. Complications were more common after surgery (OR 7.5; 95% CI, 2.0-42). Another RCT randomized patients with displaced intra-articular calcaneal fracture to minimally invasive longitudinal approach with a sinus tarsi approach. There were fewer complications with the minimally invasive technique, although outcomes were better for Sanders type IV fractures with the sinus tarsi approach.

A systematic review identified five RCTs with 707 patients comparing cannulated screw fixation vs plate fixation for intra-articular calcaneal fracture. Outcomes were similar, other than shorter duration of surgery and fewer complications (RR 0.25; 95% CI, 0.15-0.44) with cannulated screw fixation.

A systematic review of 6 retrospective cohort studies with 247 patients found that robotic assisted percutaneous hollow screw fixation surgery had generally similar outcomes to traditional open reduction internal fixation surgery for patients with calcaneal fracture.

A systematic review of 5 retrospective studies with 473 feet of patients with displaced intra-articular calcaneal fracture found similar outcomes for intramedullary nail versus conventional plate surgery.

A systematic review identified 14 RCTs with 1367 patients comparing minimally invasive surgery with the extensile lateral approach. They found fewer wound complications with minimally invasive surgery, better functional scores, and similar radiologic outcomes.
The data regarding robot assisted surgery for calcaneal fracture are limited.
Any intra-articular fracture with greater than 25% involvement of the joint surface should be referred for surgical treatment.
Fractures of the second to fifth metatarsal shaft with at least 3 mm displacement or greater than 10º angulation warrant surgical referral for reduction.

A clinical trial of patients with Zone 1 fifth metatarsal base fracture found uniformly good results whether patients received operative or non-operative therapy, even among those with a fracture gap greater than 2 mm.

In patients with 2 to 3 mm displaced avulsion fractures of the base of the 5th metatarsal, those randomized to operative treatment had better short-term but not long-term outcomes than those in the non-operative group.

A randomized trial compared treatment of 5th metatarsal base fracture with a double elasticated bandage with below knee walking cast, and found no significant difference in outcomes at 1 and 6 months.
A systematic review comparing removable splint with cast for treatment of 5th metatarsal fracture found better results with the removable splint.

For patients with Zone 2 or 3 fifth metatarsal base fractures, rates of non-union are higher and operative therapy should be considered, especially in more active persons and athletes in which evidence shows earlier return to activity with surgical management.

A systematic review of 10 observational studies with 390 patients with spiral oblique fracture of the 5th metatarsal ("dancer's fracture") found low quality evidence of comparable outcomes with operative versus non-operative management. Operative management may allow earlier return to sport.

A systematic review identified eight studies with 200 patients of operative vs non-operative therapy for navicular fracture. Surgery provided an earlier return to sport (16 vs 22 weeks) but firm conclusions of the value of one approach over another could not be drawn.

The great toe has an increased role in weight bearing and balance; thus, fractures with any degree of displacement, angulation, or rotational deformity should be considered for referral and possible surgical managment.
Greater toe fractures may be treated with a short leg walking boot or cast for 2-3 weeks, then a rigid-sole shoe for an additional 3-4 weeks.
Treatment for the majority of lesser toe fractures only requires buddy taping and a rigid-sole for 4-6 weeks with progressive ambulation as tolerated. B
A systematic review of 23 observational comparative studies found no difference between primary arthrodesis or open reduction internal fixation, but this must be considered very low quality evidence.

Early treatment of navicular stress fractures with NWBSLC for 6 to 8 weeks has an 86% success rate with return to activity at 5.6 months. All other conservative treatments excluding NWBSLC have a success rate of 38% with return to activity at 9.3 months. Surgical intervention had a similar success rate to NWBSLC at 83%, but has quicker average return to activity of 3.8 months.

Navicular stress fractures and small nondisplaced avulsions may be managed conservatively, but close follow-up is necessary to identify possible complications of delayed healing, nonunion, and avascular necrosis.

Refer most calcaneal and talus fractures excluding small extra-articular avulsions for consideration of surgical management. However, an abundance of RCT's and inconclusive meta-analysis highlight the fact that no single approach can be applied to these type of fractures.
Treatment of common metatarsal fractures is summarized in , and treatment of common tarsal fractures is summarized in
Refer all open fractures emergently. Also, urgent surgical referral is required for displaced posterior calcaneal tuberosity avulsion fractures.

Consider referral for toe (phalanx) fractures that include a fracture-dislocation, displaced intra-articular frature, nondisplaced intra-articular fractures involving more than 25% of the joint, and physis (growth plate) fractures.

Due to the high functional demands and potential for articular surface damage, surgical referral is recommended within 1 to 3 days for most tarsal fractures, excluding small, nondisplaced avulsions and conservatively managed stress fractures.

Refer fifth metatarsal tuberosity avulsion fractures if there is greater than 3 mm of displacment, if step-off is greater than 1-2 mm on the cuboid articular surface, or if a fragment inclues greater than 60% of the metatarsal-cuboid joint surface.

Individuals with Jones fractures should be referred if the patient is an athlete or highly active, if there is greater than 2 mm of displacement, or if conservative therapy is ineffective after 12 weeks of immobilization and radiography reveals nonunion.
Refer patients with diastasis greater than 2 mm between the first and second metatarsals, gross instability, or fractures of the Lisfranc joint for surgical reduction and stabilization.
For control of pain and swelling, consider hospital admission for most acute calcaneus fractures.
Healing of metatarsal fractures typically progresses well, and complications such as symptomatic nonunion occur infrequently. C

Management of toe fractures is influenced by the severity of the injury and the patient's activity level, but most involve minimal displacement and fully heal without need for surgical intervention. In an analysis of 339 toe fractures, 95% involved less than 2 mm of displacement and all fractures were managed conservatively with good outcomes.
Stress fractures of the metatarsal shaft usually heal well without immobilization and typically respond well to cessation of the causative activity for 4 to 8 weeks. B
Nonoperative management of Lisfranc injuries with a diastasis greater than 2 mm typically portends an inferior prognosis than surgical fixation. A
